In the event a disaster affects the company, the third-party or our customers, the business could be harmed.

AMD completed its acquisition of Xilinx on February,2022, which allowed AMD to have access to a new set of markets and customers, further strengthening and diversifying their business. Added FPGAs and adaptative SoC to its portfolio.

Qualcomm reports three segments and operates primarily through two: QCT, the semiconductor business that develops and supplies integrated circuits and system software, and QTL, the licensing business that grants rights to its intellectual property portfolio

Micron identifies volatility in average selling prices as a primary risk: it and its competitors continually expand capacity, improve yields and shrink die size, so worldwide supply can rise faster than demand and push prices down.

Broadcom has two reportable segments: semiconductor solutions, which includes all its product lines and intellectual property licensing, and infrastructure software, which includes its mainframe, distributed and cyber security solutions and its fibre channel storage area networking business.

NVIDIA builds inventory ahead of anticipated demand and enters long-term supply and capacity commitments, so misjudging demand creates mismatches in either direction: it may fail to secure enough capacity, or be left with commitments it no longer needs. At the end of fiscal 2023 purchase obligations and prepaid supply agreements represented more than half of its total supply, and it warns it may incur inventory provisions if inventory or supply commitments are misaligned with demand.

In the Data Center segment AMD says it competes primarily against Intel with its server CPUs and against NVIDIA with its GPU and DPU products. It adds that fabless companies offer proprietary accelerators and Arm-based CPUs for data center use, and that some of its own customers are internally developing their own data center processors and accelerators, which could shrink AMD's available market.

Qualcomm derives a significant portion of both its chip revenues and its licensing revenues from a small number of customers and licensees, especially from their sales of premium tier handsets. Despite having more than 300 licensees, a limited number of them, including several Chinese OEMs, account for much of licensing revenue. It warns that the concentration of device share among few companies gives those buyers purchasing power that can push its prices, revenues and margins down.

Micron's portfolio is based on three semiconductor memory and storage technologies: DRAM, NAND and NOR. From these it builds products including managed NAND, solid-state drives and other memory systems, sold under the Micron and Crucial brands.

Broadcom states that acquiring businesses is part of its growth strategy and that these deals, including the VMware merger, carry integration risk: due diligence may fail to surface problems with the acquired business's products, financial disclosures, accounting practices or legal and tax contingencies, and integrating operations and retaining personnel may prove difficult. For VMware specifically it warns that if customers reject the shift from perpetual to subscription licensing and the simplified portfolio, the investment may yield little value and significant customers may be lost.

The disclosure escalates from generic to specific and from hypothetical to actual. In fiscal 2022 NVIDIA mentions export controls only in general terms, tied to Russia sanctions and to the risk of being found in violation of export laws; controls on AI chips do not appear. Fiscal 2023 introduces them as a possibility, saying semiconductors associated with AI including GPUs are increasingly the focus of export control restrictions. By fiscal 2024 the same language becomes "export controls targeting GPUs and semiconductors associated with AI, which have been imposed and are increasingly likely to be further tightened", and mentions rise from three chunks to fourteen.

AMD's 2021 risk factors do not mention artificial intelligence at all. By fiscal 2023 a dedicated risk factor appears stating that issues related to the responsible use of AI may result in reputational, competitive and financial harm and liability, and by fiscal year 2024 the risk focus on the incresing regulatory restrictions targeting products and services enabling or facilitating AI , which could harm their AI related products

In 2022 and 2023 Micron lists CHIPS Act grants and tax credits as expected support for its two new US memory fabs. In 2024 it has signed a non-binding preliminary agreement with the Commerce Department for a grant but warns it may not result in funding, and the risk bullet changes from "ability" to "inability" to realize those grants.

In both years Apple, Samsung and Xiaomi each account for 10% or more of Qualcomm's consolidated revenues. What changes is how Qualcomm names the threat: in 2021 it warns of competition from products internally developed by "some of our largest customers" without naming them, while in 2024 it names Apple and Samsung explicitly as customers developing competing products.

In fiscal 2021 NVIDIA attributes Data Center growth of 124% to the Mellanox acquisition and the ramp of the Ampere GPU architecture. By fiscal 2024 the Data Center is its central platform and the disclosure is dominated by export restrictions: sales to China fell from 19% to 14% of Data Center revenue, and NVIDIA reports it has not received licenses to ship restricted products there.

AMD completed the Xilinx acquisition on February 14, 2022, paying $48.5 billion in stock, with $27.3 billion allocated to intangible assets and $22.8 billion to goodwill. Acquisition-related costs were $350 million in 2022, $26 million in 2023 and immaterial in 2024, and by 2024 Xilinx appears as historical figures: $4,612 million of net revenue and $2,247 million of operating income in 2022.

In fiscal year 2024 AMD, Broadcom and Intel mention TSMC. AMD rely on TSMC to manufacture their products, and insufficient supply could materially affect the business. Broadcom says TSMC produced about 95% of the wafers made by its contract manufacturers and notes TSMC also serves competitors and could prioritize them. ntel states its most advanced products are either exclusively manufactured by TSMC or rely on critical components made by TSMC.

Neither describes competition in AI accelerators as a separate topic; both frame it within general competition. NVIDIA anchors its position in the full-stack platform, listing software support, conformity to industry standard APIs and breadth of product offerings among the principal competitive factors and stressing that its large body of software including CUDA is what makes its chips a platform. AMD frames competition around market dynamics, warning that competitors may adapt faster and that the AI market is subject to rapid technological change and product obsolescence, while pointing to strong demand for its Instinct MI300X accelerators.

Broadcom quantifies the risk in detail: sales to distributors were 48% of net revenue in fiscal 2024, direct sales to one distributor were 28%, and its top five end customers accounted for about 40%, up from 35% in 2023, with loss of a significant customer listed as a demand risk. Micron discloses far less: about half of total revenue came from its top ten customers and one customer accounted for 10% of total revenue in 2024.

AMD, NVIDIA and Broadcom describe export restrictions as a material risk in fiscal 2023. AMD warns that new export control restrictions imposed by the US, China or other countries could materially affect its business and impede its R&D teams outside the US. NVIDIA says export controls targeting GPUs and semiconductors associated with AI are increasingly likely and would restrict its exports while competitors may not face the same limits. Broadcom cites US export restrictions on its customer Huawei, which forced it to suspend sales pending Commerce Department licences.

Both are fabless, but Qualcomm is a partial exception. AMD states it uses third-party wafer foundries for all of its products, relying on TSMC for all microprocessor and GPU wafers at 7nm or smaller nodes. Qualcomm says QCT uses a fabless production model and does not own or operate foundries, except for certain RFFE modules and RF filter products, whose front-end manufacturing it runs itself in Germany and Singapore; it flags the higher fixed costs that owning those facilities implies relative to a fabless model.
AMD does not own fabs and relies on TSMC to manufacture its products; a disruption or capacity shortage at TSMC would directly limit AMD's ability to supply.

Micron cites the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 as support for building two leading-edge memory fabs in the United States, funded through grants and investment tax credits, and reached preliminary terms with the U.S. Department of Commerce for a grant. It flags the risk that those preliminary terms may not result in actual funding.

mellanox is a supllier of high-performance interconnect products for computing. Nvidia adquired all outstanding shares of mellanox. Revenue growth was driven by the mellanox acquisition and contributed 10% of total company revenue

Qualcomm acquired Nuvia in March 2021 for $1.1 billion in cash. The filings discuss Nuvia mainly because Arm sued Qualcomm and Nuvia in August 2022, alleging that after the acquisition they breached Nuvia's Architecture License Agreement. The filings do not describe what Nuvia's business was.

NVIDIA's total revenue for fiscal 2024 was $60,922 million, or $60.9 billion, up 126% from fiscal 2023.
AMD spent $5,872 million on research and development in fiscal 2023, or $5.9 billion, an increase of $867 million or 17% over the $5.0 billion spent in 2022.

Micron's consolidated gross margin was negative 9% in fiscal 2023, down from 45% in 2022. In dollars it was negative $1,416 million on revenue of $15,540 million, driven by inventory write-downs to net realizable value as DRAM and NAND selling prices fell.
Broadcom repurchased and retired approximately 67 million shares in fiscal 2024 for $7,176 million

Qualcomm's QTL licensing segment revenue was $5,572 million in fiscal 2024, up $266 million from $5,306 million in 2023, with EBT of $4,027 million or 72% of segment revenues. This is distinct from the $6,171 million "Licensing" line in the consolidated statements of operations, which is broader than the QTL segment.
NVIDIA's Data Center revenue was $15.01 billion in fiscal 2023 and grew 217% in fiscal 2024.

Broadcom and Intel report both. Broadcom states TSMC manufactured about 95% of the wafers made by its contract manufacturers in fiscal 2024, and separately reports that its top five end customers accounted for about 40% of net revenue. Intel reports that its most advanced products are exclusively manufactured by TSMC or rely on critical components from TSMC, and discloses a concentration of revenue in its three largest customers. AMD reports the TSMC dependence in these candidates but not customer concentration.

The two framings barely touch. As opportunity, AI is concrete and quantified: Data Center revenue of $47.5 billion in fiscal 2024, up 217%, new inference platforms for generative AI and LLMs, paid NVIDIA AI Enterprise licences, the DGX Cloud training service and 4.7 million CUDA developers. As risk, AI is abstract and societal: NVIDIA says AI poses emerging legal, social and ethical issues that could affect its adoption and therefore its business, and lists the responsible use of AI among regulatory requirements whose compliance can be onerous and expensive. It does not quantify the risk side at all.

Yes. AMD discusses both in fiscal 2023 and 2024, Intel in 2023 and 2024, and Micron in 2022, 2023 and 2024. Micron combines them most heavily, with the CHIPS Act appearing across sixteen chunks of its 2024 filing alongside ten on export restrictions. The two topics are opposite sides of the same policy: CHIPS Act incentives to build fabs in the United States, and export controls limiting what can be sold to China.

AMD completed Xilinx in February 2022 and Silo AI in August 2024, with ZT Systems pending. NVIDIA completed Mellanox in April 2020 and separately took a $1.36 billion write-off on the terminated Arm transaction. Intel completed four acquisitions in 2021 and six in 2020. Qualcomm acquired Veoneer, paying a $110 million termination fee to Magna. The integration risks reported are generic and largely shared: funding, assumption of liabilities, integration challenges, increased debt, legal proceedings arising from the acquisition, and failure of due diligence to identify significant issues.
